families.title: Bridge Courier
families.rules: Move along drawn roads without teleporting. Dots are junctions; crossings without dots are not junctions. Revisit dots freely. When the goal says exactly once, use each road once. For a distance target, cover every road, return to the marked depot, and meet the target; repeats are allowed. All roads are undirected. Every unlabelled road has length 1.
families.mathematics: Euler trails, degree parity, cycle splicing, bridges, and the undirected route-inspection (Chinese postman) problem. The change from exact-once to shortest delivery explicitly introduces necessary repetition. Pairing odd vertices explains the optimization; no proof answer is required.

families.authoring_policy: Use named constructions and deliberate structural contrasts. Tutorial 1 can be skipped. Choose endpoints, bridges, or weights to reveal one intended decision; do not hide randomly forbidden roads. Accept every route meeting the goal.

instances.title: The little side road
instances.prompt: Choose where to start. Walk every road exactly once. You may visit a dot again.

parameters.construction: Square A–B–C–D–A with one leaf E joined to A.

instances.hint: Try starting at the end of the little side road.
instances.insight: A dead end must be an endpoint of the whole walk; the repeated visit to A is legal.
instances.prerequisites: No reading with narration; track five used edges.
instances.difficulty: Entry/tutorial; the decision is choosing a viable start, not counting a large map. Let a confident child skip it.
instances.author_certificate: Five roads; exactly A and E have odd degree. A complete trail therefore has endpoints A and E. Witness uses every road once.

instances.title: Do the small loop before home
instances.prompt: Start at B. Walk every road exactly once and finish back at B.

parameters.construction: A square A–B–C–D–A and a triangle A–E–F–A share just A.

instances.hint: When you reach A, take the triangle detour before using your last road home.
instances.insight: Splice a complete loop into a larger route; returning home too early can strand unused roads.
instances.prerequisites: Track seven used edges; no arithmetic or graph terms required.
instances.difficulty: Early planning; one real choice at the shared junction can end the walk too soon. This is a loop-splicing lesson, not an enlarged path.
instances.author_certificate: Seven roads; all degrees even. For example B–C–D–A–E–F–A–B covers all seven exactly once.

instances.title: Cross the connecting bridge at the right time
instances.prompt: Start at C. Walk every road exactly once. You may finish at a different dot.

parameters.construction: Two triangles A–B–C–A and D–E–F–D, joined only by C–D.

instances.hint: If you cross C–D now, can you ever return to unfinished roads on the left?
instances.insight: A bridge separates two regions: finish the departing side before the unique crossing.
instances.prerequisites: Track seven edges; plan which region to finish first.
instances.difficulty: Planning; the tempting first move C→D loses immediately despite looking locally legal. Same edge count as instance 2, different insight.
instances.author_certificate: Seven roads; odd vertices C,D force endpoints. The bridge can be crossed only once, after servicing the left triangle and before servicing the right.

instances.title: Three corridors, one depot
instances.prompt: Start at S. Travel every road at least once and return to S in 8 steps. Roads can be repeated.

parameters.construction: Three internally disjoint length-two paths S–A–T, S–B–T, S–C–T (a subdivided three-edge theta graph).

instances.hint: You will have used three corridors to reach the far end. Which corridor will get you home?
instances.insight: Repetition is now allowed because the destination is a shortest closed delivery tour, not an Euler trail. One entire corridor must be repeated.
instances.prerequisites: Count to 8; distinguish used-once from used-again roads.
instances.difficulty: Optimization entry; identify a necessary return trip instead of searching for an impossible six-step closed route.
instances.author_certificate: Base length 6. S,T are odd. Extra traversals must connect them; their distance is 2, so minimum cost 8. Duplicating any one corridor attains it.

instances.title: Ladder delivery
instances.prompt: Start at A. Cover every road and return to A in 12 steps. Every road costs 1 step.

parameters.construction: The ordinary ladder graph with top rail A–B–C–D, bottom rail a–b–c–d, and four aligned rungs.

instances.hint: The four middle junctions each have three roads. Try repeating the two middle rungs.
instances.insight: Repair odd degrees in pairs; two well-chosen repeats beat treating every road as an out-and-back errand.
instances.prerequisites: Count to 12; coordinate four junctions and undo route choices.
instances.difficulty: Intermediate optimization; either pair the middle junctions vertically or horizontally. Both natural optimal plans are accepted.
instances.author_certificate: Base length 10; B,C,b,c are odd. One extra edge changes degree parity at two ends, so at least two repeats are necessary. Repeating B–b and C–c attains 12.

instances.title: Choose the roads to repeat
instances.prompt: Start at A. Cover every road and return to A with total distance 22. Each traversal costs the number written on its road, including repeats.

parameters.construction: Complete graph on four junctions: every pair has a road. Road lengths AB=1, AC=2, AD=3, BC=3, BD=2, CD=7. Draw D inside triangle ABC so every junction is unambiguous.

instances.hint: Plan both extra connections before committing to repeating the cheapest road. Long roads still need one delivery.
instances.insight: Pairing odd junctions is a global choice. Selecting AB as a repeated connection leaves an expensive extra connection between C and D. Starting the route along AB can still be optimal; the choice here is which roads to repeat. Shortest extra connections may use multiple roads.
instances.prerequisites: Add small positive lengths up to 22; compare complete plans.
instances.difficulty: Stretch; six roads suffice to create a genuine optimization trap. The weights distinguish choosing both extra connections together from selecting the cheapest extra connection first, with no legal-road exclusions.
instances.author_certificate: Base cost 18. All four junctions are odd. Shortest pairing costs AB + CD = 1 + 5 = 6, AC + BD = 2 + 2 = 4, AD + BC = 3 + 3 = 6. Minimum augmentation 4 yields 22; repeating AC and BD attains it. Selecting AB as an extra connection leaves C and D paired at shortest distance 5, hence augmentation 6. This concerns extra traversals, not the order in which the required roads are first visited.

instances.title: Choose the house endpoints

parameters.construction: A square with a triangular roof.

instances.hint: Only two junctions have an odd number of roads. Start at one of them.
instances.insight: An Euler trail can revisit junctions while using each road once; the endpoints are forced by degree parity.
instances.prerequisites: Track connections and revise a plan; line crossings are not junctions.
instances.difficulty_reasoning: An Euler trail can revisit junctions while using each road once; the endpoints are forced by degree parity.
instances.provenance: App adaptation of the house graph and Euler-trail task in Week 10 middle/facilitator sources. The graph is borrowed; app interaction and hint are newly written.

instances.insight: Returning home early can strand a whole loop; splice all three cycles into one closed walk.

instances.insight: Six odd vertices require at least three extra crossings; a matching attains the bound on this prism.

instances.hint: You must cross the long direct road once. For the extra trip between A and B, compare whole paths.
instances.insight: The shortest parity repair can use two roads even when a direct road exists. Required coverage and cheapest repeats are different choices.

instances.hint: Compare complete pairings of all six odd junctions; the cheapest single road does not choose the other two pairs for you.
instances.insight: Weighted six-vertex matching combines parity with shortest-path costs; an optimal augmentation must be planned globally.

families.title: Neighbor Lanterns
families.rules: Color every dot with the supplied palette. The endpoints of every drawn link must have different colors. Recolor freely; no fixed clues, color quotas, or one-off restrictions. A crossing without a dot is not a junction. Color dots, not links.
families.mathematics: Proper vertex coloring and chromatic number; bipartition, odd-cycle closure, wheels, graph powers, and the Petersen graph. The supplied palette is minimal, checked exhaustively. The player only has to produce a coloring, never a proof of minimality.

families.authoring_policy: One optional path tutorial, then changes in structure rather than larger checkerboards. The six instances are a sequence of reusable ideas, not a promise that each will take longer than the preceding one. Test completion and recoloring behavior with children.

instances.title: A line of lanterns
instances.prompt: Color all five lanterns with the two colors. Linked lanterns must differ.

parameters.construction: Path A–B–C–D–E.

instances.hint: Try alternating the two colors.
instances.insight: Two-coloring propagates along a path. This teaches the interaction, not the main difficulty.
instances.prerequisites: Distinguish two colors or shape patterns; no reading or counting.
instances.difficulty: Optional tutorial, deliberately easy. Do not fill a grade trail with resized copies of it.
instances.author_certificate: Any edge forces two colors; alternating is a witness.

instances.title: Closing the necklace
instances.prompt: Color the five-lantern ring using these three colors. Linked lanterns must differ.

parameters.construction: Cycle A–B–C–D–E–A.

instances.hint: Remember that the last lantern is also linked to the first.
instances.insight: An odd loop breaks perfect alternation; reserve a third color for the closure.
instances.prerequisites: Notice the closing edge; willing to recolor.
instances.difficulty: Early; introduces a global closure decision after the tutorial. Three colors allow several answers, all accepted.
instances.author_certificate: With only two colors, alternating around five edges returns the wrong color to the start. Three colors suffice.

instances.title: The hub needs a color
instances.prompt: Color the square and its center using three colors. Each spoke and rim link joins different colors.

parameters.construction: Wheel with rim A–B–C–D–A and hub H linked to every rim vertex; rim size 4.

instances.hint: Set a color aside for the center, then color the rim.
instances.insight: The hub must avoid every rim color, so the rim has to share colors strategically.
instances.prerequisites: Coordinate the four rim dots with the center.
instances.difficulty: Early planning; freely using all three colors on the rim can block the center. Coloring the center first turns the remaining rim into a two-color task.
instances.author_certificate: A hub and two adjacent rim vertices form a triangle, forcing 3. Alternating the even rim with colors 1 and 2 leaves 3 for H.

author_checks.explanation: The rim uses all three colors, leaving none for H.
author_checks.scope: Design evidence only; these are not fixed clues in the playable instance.

instances.title: One more corner changes the wheel
instances.prompt: Color the pentagon and its center using four colors. Each spoke and rim link joins different colors.

parameters.construction: Wheel with rim A–B–C–D–E–A and hub H linked to every rim vertex; rim size 5.

instances.hint: First solve the five-lantern rim. The center touches every rim lantern.
instances.insight: Combine two earlier ideas: the odd rim needs three colors, and the hub needs another.
instances.prerequisites: Recall odd-ring closure; coordinate center and rim.
instances.difficulty: Structural contrast, not a size ramp: one added rim vertex changes the necessary palette from 3 to 4. Still short; advance quickly if solved immediately.
instances.author_certificate: The odd rim needs 3 colors. Its universal hub cannot use any rim color, forcing 4. An odd-cycle coloring plus a new hub color attains 4.

author_checks.explanation: The rim uses all four colors, leaving none for H.
author_checks.scope: Design evidence only; these are not fixed clues in the playable instance.

instances.title: Two neighbors each way
instances.prompt: Color the eight-lantern ring with four colors. Every drawn link must join different colors. Links reach the next lantern and the one after it in each direction.

parameters.construction: Square of the 8-cycle: labels 1…8 clockwise; link labels whose circular distance is 1 or 2. No other links.

instances.hint: Any three consecutive lanterns need three different colors. Watch what happens when your pattern meets itself around the ring.
instances.insight: A local three-color pattern can fail globally. Uniform longer-range adjacency creates the challenge, rather than arbitrary forbidden pairs.
instances.prerequisites: Trace next-nearest links and coordinate a whole ring; no arithmetic required if links are drawn.
instances.difficulty: Intermediate/stretch; decisions interact two positions ahead and across the closing seam. A repeated block of four colors works; many other valid colorings are allowed.
instances.author_certificate: Every three consecutive vertices form a triangle. With only 3 colors, each next color is forced to repeat the color three positions earlier. That period cannot close on length 8. Pattern 1,2,3,4,1,2,3,4 is valid, so the minimum is 4.

author_checks.explanation: This legal five-dot prefix has no completion with four colors; later links across the seam force a recoloring.
author_checks.scope: Design evidence only; these are not fixed clues in the playable instance.

instances.title: Pentagon and star
instances.prompt: Color all ten lanterns with three colors. Every link joins different colors. Line crossings have no lantern and do not add connections.

parameters.construction: Petersen graph: outer pentagon o0–o1–o2–o3–o4–o0; inner star links i0–i2–i4–i1–i3–i0; five matching spokes oj–ij.

instances.hint: The inside is also a five-lantern loop, just drawn as a star. Color both loops while watching their five spokes.
instances.insight: Two odd loops can share three colors, but their colorings must agree with all matching spokes. This is a compact graph with interacting global choices.
instances.prerequisites: Track connections through a crossing drawing; revise several colors when necessary.
instances.difficulty: Stretch; ten vertices give coupled cycles and real backtracking without a large board or extra rule types. The drawing must make non-junction crossings clear.
instances.author_certificate: The outer 5-cycle rules out 2 colors. The stored 3-color assignment checks every one of 15 links, hence the minimum is 3. It is vertex coloring; the separate Petersen edge-coloring problem is not being claimed here.

author_checks.explanation: The outer ring and two inner colors are locally legal, but no choice for the remaining inner dots can satisfy all links with three colors.
author_checks.scope: Design evidence only; these are not fixed clues in the playable instance.

instances.hint: Alternate around each square, then check the four joining links.
instances.insight: Two even cycles must use compatible phases across their matching links.

instances.title: A fourth color without a triangle

parameters.construction: Mycielski construction on the 5-cycle: uppercase cycle, independent lowercase neighbor copies, and X adjacent to all copies.

instances.hint: The center links to every lowercase dot. Try sharing its color with selected uppercase dots, then coordinate both rings.
instances.insight: Copying each cycle vertex’s neighbors and adding a common neighbor forces a fourth color even though there is no triangle. The complete graph is small enough to check by search.
